name: Cerebellar Ataxia, Neuropathy and Vestibular Areflexia Syndrome
aliases: Cerebellar ataxia, neuropathy, vestibular areflexia syndrome (CANVAS, RFC1)

clinicalPearls: Late-onset autosomal recessive multisystem disorder most often caused by a biallelic intronic pentanucleotide repeat expansion in RFC1, usually in an AAGGG configuration.
Classically defined by the triad of cerebellar ataxia, a sensory neuronopathy (ganglionopathy) and bilateral vestibular impairment.
A chronic dry cough frequently precedes the neurological features by years to decades and is a valuable diagnostic clue.
The sensory deficit is a non-length-dependent ganglionopathy, so sensory loss can involve the face, trunk and limbs in a patchy distribution.
Bilateral vestibular failure produces oscillopsia and an abnormal visually-enhanced vestibulo-ocular reflex that can be demonstrated at the bedside.
Dysautonomia, including orthostatic symptoms and altered sweating, is increasingly recognised within the RFC1 spectrum.
RFC1 expansions can produce phenotypes broader than the full triad, including isolated sensory neuronopathy or a later-onset cerebellar syndrome.
Onset is usually in mid-to-late adult life and progression is characteristically slow.
reference.pathophysiology: CANVAS is most commonly driven by a biallelic intronic repeat expansion in RFC1, which encodes a subunit of the replication factor C complex involved in DNA replication and repair. The expansion is thought to impair normal gene expression or RNA handling, and although the exact downstream mechanism is still being defined, the result is a slowly progressive degeneration of several populations of sensory and balance-related neurons. Dorsal root ganglion neurons degenerate to produce a non-length-dependent sensory neuronopathy, the vestibular ganglia and their projections degenerate to cause bilateral vestibular failure, and cerebellar involvement adds an ataxic component. The chronic cough that so often precedes overt neurological disease is attributed to involvement of sensory afferents supplying the airway, producing a hypersensitive cough reflex. The combined loss of proprioceptive, vestibular and cerebellar inputs explains the profound imbalance that characterises established disease.
additionalDifferentials: Toxic ganglionopathy from platinum agents or pyridoxine excess
Friedreich ataxia and other hereditary ataxias
Multiple system atrophy of cerebellar type
Late-onset spinocerebellar ataxias without RFC1 expansion
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies showing a non-length-dependent sensory neuronopathy with reduced or absent sensory responses
Video head impulse test and caloric testing demonstrating bilateral vestibular hypofunction
Brain and spinal MRI assessing cerebellar atrophy and dorsal column change
Dedicated RFC1 repeat-expansion testing (flanking and repeat-primed PCR, with Southern blot where needed)
Screening for acquired ganglionopathy including autoimmune, paraneoplastic and Sjogren workup
Autonomic function testing where dysautonomia is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly progressive sensory loss suggesting an acquired paraneoplastic ganglionopathy
Recurrent falls with injury from combined sensory and vestibular loss
reference.prognosis: The disorder progresses slowly over decades, with disability accruing from the combined sensory, vestibular and cerebellar deficits. Life expectancy is generally not markedly shortened, though falls and immobility contribute to morbidity.
pitfalls: Dismissing a long-standing chronic cough as unrelated respiratory disease rather than a clue to CANVAS.
Labelling a sensory neuronopathy as idiopathic without testing for the RFC1 expansion.
Attributing imbalance solely to cerebellar disease and failing to test the vestibulo-ocular reflex for bilateral vestibular failure.
Relying on standard sequencing panels, which miss the intronic repeat, when dedicated repeat-expansion testing is required.
references: Hereditary ataxia and neuro-otology reference reviews
